title: Time and Work

steps.title: Think in work rates
steps.content: If a person finishes a job in n days, their one-day work rate is 1/n of the job. When people work together, add their rates—not their completion times.
steps.formula:
Rate = 1 ÷ Days
Combined rate = Rate A + Rate B
steps.example: A takes 6 days, B takes 3 days. Together rate = 1/6+1/3 = 1/2 job/day, so they finish in 2 days.
steps.tip: Never add the number of days. Always convert to work per day first.

steps.title: Combine two workers
steps.prompt: A finishes a job in 10 days and B in 15 days. How long do they take together?
hints: Convert each completion time into one-day work.
Add the rates, then take the reciprocal.

steps.title: Use total work units
steps.content: When times produce awkward fractions, choose total work as the LCM of the individual days. Work per day becomes an integer and combined time is easier.
steps.example: A = 12 days, B = 18 days. Total work = 36 units. A does 3/day, B does 2/day; together 5/day → 36/5 = 7.2 days.
steps.tip: If one worker leaves, subtract their rate from the combined rate.

steps.title: Find the missing worker
steps.prompt: A and B together finish a job in 6 days. A alone takes 10 days. How long does B alone take?
hints: Combined rate minus A's rate isolates B.
Take the reciprocal of B's rate to get days.

steps.title: Work and efficiency
steps.content: For the same job, efficiency is inversely proportional to time. If A is twice as efficient as B, A takes half the time B takes.
steps.example: If B takes 20 days and A is twice as efficient, A takes 10 days.

steps.title: Trace a combined rate
steps.content: Add rates carefully with a common denominator.
steps.prompt: A takes 5 days and B takes 20 days. How many days do they take together?
steps.explanation: Combined rate is 1/4 job per day, so they finish in 4 days.
hints: Convert both times to fractions of work per day.
Add the fractions before taking the reciprocal.

steps.title: Solve a two-worker problem
steps.content: A reliable order prevents the common mistake of adding days.
steps.prompt: Arrange the steps for A = 12 days and B = 12 days working together.
options: Take reciprocal of combined rate to get 6 days
steps.explanation: Times → rates → sum of rates → reciprocal time.
hints: The answer is a time, so invert the combined rate at the end.

steps.title: Efficiency ratio
steps.prompt: If A is 3 times as efficient as B, and B takes 18 days, A takes:
steps.explanation: Time is inversely proportional to efficiency. A takes 18/3 = 6 days.
hints: Divide B's time by the efficiency ratio.

steps.title: Catch the add-the-days error
steps.content: A student says A (10 days) and B (15 days) together take 25 days.
steps.prompt: What is wrong with that answer?
options: Days must not be added; rates 1/10 and 1/15 combine to finish in 6 days
Together they always take the slower worker's time
Together they always take the faster worker's time

feedback_by_option.1: Correct. Combined rate = 1/6, so time = 6 days.
feedback_by_option.2: 5 days is too fast for these rates.
feedback_by_option.3: Working together is faster than either alone.
feedback_by_option.4: Working together is faster than the faster worker alone as well.

steps.explanation: Always convert to rates before combining workers.
hints: Ask what fraction of the job each person finishes per day.
Add those fractions, not the day counts.

learning_objectives: Represent a worker's speed as a fraction of work per unit time.
Relate efficiency ratios to completion times.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Add the number of days to combine workers.
common_misconceptions.correction: Add work rates; completion times are reciprocals of rates.

common_misconceptions.misconception: A faster worker has a larger time per job.
common_misconceptions.correction: A faster worker completes a larger fraction of the job per unit time.

common_misconceptions.misconception: If half the work is complete, half the time always remains.
common_misconceptions.correction: Remaining time depends on the rate of the workers still doing the job.

worked_examples.title: Combine two workers
worked_examples.explanation: Add rates because both contribute work at the same time.

worked_examples.title: Find one worker's rate
worked_examples.explanation: Subtract known rates to isolate the unknown worker.

worked_examples.title: Efficiency ratio
worked_examples.explanation: Higher efficiency means less time for the same work.

company_applications.practice: Convert each completion time to a rate before combining.
Handle a worker leaving by calculating remaining work.
Use a common total-work unit to avoid fraction mistakes.
Translate efficiency ratios into time ratios quickly.

srs_cards.question: How do you find a one-day work rate?
srs_cards.answer: If a worker completes a job in n days, the one-day rate is 1/n of the job.

srs_cards.question: How do two workers' rates combine?
srs_cards.answer: Add their work completed per unit time, then take the reciprocal to find the time for one whole job.

srs_cards.question: Why must you not add the number of days?
srs_cards.answer: Days are not additive work contributions; rates are.

quest.story: Service-company papers punish students who add days instead of rates. Build every answer from work per day.
quest.mission: Represent work as rates, combine workers and calculate completion time.
success_criteria: Convert completion time into a one-day work rate.
Add rates for workers working together.
